summary: This informational document looks at the fixed 64-bit boundary in IPv6 unicast addresses, where the first part identifies the subnet and the last part identifies the interface. It describes the advantages of keeping the boundary fixed and examines the issues that would arise if it were made variable.

eli5.summary: An IPv6 address is like a street address: half says which street, half says which house. This note explains why always splitting it in the middle is handy, and what would get messy if the split could move.

questions: can i use a prefix longer than /64
subtitle: Why IPv6 subnets are fixed at /64, and what would break if the boundary between prefix and interface identifier could move.

tldr.problem: IPv6 routing works with prefixes of any length up to /128, yet almost every IPv6 interface identifier is 64 bits, so subnets are fixed at /64. People often ask why, and some want longer prefixes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the benefits of a fixed 64-bit identifier, examines arguments for shorter ones, and analyses effects on specifications, implementations, privacy and security.
tldr.outcome: It concludes that the IETF consensus is that keeping the length fixed at 64 bits outweighs the arguments for change, though it makes no proposal about the length.

today: RFC 7421 is an Informational RFC and nothing in the unit metadata says it has been obsoleted or updated. It explains the reasoning and states the IETF consensus, but makes no proposal to change the IID length.

sections.title: Where the 64-bit Boundary Comes From
sections.content:
An IPv6 unicast address is n bits of subnet prefix followed by (128-n) bits of interface identifier (IID). Routing protocols support prefixes of any length up to /128, and neither SLAAC nor DHCPv6 fixes the length. Yet RFC 4291, as modified by RFC 7136, requires IIDs of 64 bits for all unicast addresses except those starting with binary 000.

The /64 boundary was introduced after the original design, following a period when /80 was expected. Two motivations are named: the "8+8" proposal that led to ILNP, and the expectation that 64-bit EUI-64 addresses would become widespread. The only documented exception is RFC 6164, which standardizes 127-bit prefixes on router-to-router point-to-point links. The document makes no proposal to change the IID length.
sections.eli5: The street/house split was first expected in a different place, then moved to the exact middle. Almost everything now assumes the middle.

sections.title: Advantages of a Fixed Length
sections.content:
A fixed 64-bit IID is the simplest solution for SLAAC and is consistent with the principles in RFC 5505. It also fixes the subnet prefix at 64 bits whatever aggregate prefix a site gets, which RFC 6177 says should be /56 or shorter.

  • Everything is the same: no calculating leaf subnet sizes, fewer errors.
  • Adding a subnet means taking another /64 from the pool.
  • Router configurations are homogeneous and easier to understand.
  • Documentation and training are easier.

A long identifier also makes it possible to limit host traceability by varying it, and guarantees enough addresses in any subnet. The RFC states that the IETF consensus is that the benefits of keeping 64 bits fixed outweigh the arguments for change.
sections.eli5: If every street has the same number of houses, nobody needs to do math to plan a new street. You just add another one.

sections.title: Arguments for Shorter Identifiers
sections.content:
The RFC examines four arguments and answers each.

  • Not enough space delegated: The RFC says there is no objective risk of prefix depletion from giving /48 or /56 to even the smallest sites, since only 2000::/3 is committed for unicast and about 85% of the space remains in reserve.
  • Hierarchy: A /48 already gives 16 bits for hierarchical allocation, and flat IGP routing works in large networks.
  • Audit: DHCPv6 servers already know the legitimate hosts, and ND logs cover SLAAC hosts.
  • ND cache exhaustion: A /120 would limit the address count, but 2^32 entries would still exhaust router memory, and other mitigations exist, such as those in RFC 6583. A /127 mitigates it on router point-to-point links.
sections.eli5: People say a smaller street would help with running out of room, bookkeeping or pests. The RFC explains why other fixes work without shrinking the street.

sections.title: What Breaks if the Length Varies
sections.content:
The 64-bit length appears in the addressing architecture, in many IPv6-over-foo documents (Ethernet, FDDI, IEEE 802.15.4 and more), and in specifications such as MLDv2, Teredo, 6to4 and Mobile IP home network models. Specific failure modes include:

  • IPv6 multicast addresses from unicast prefixes (RFC 3306) and embedded RP addresses assume a longest prefix of 64 bits.
  • Cryptographically Generated Addresses use 59 bits for cryptographic purposes, so a longer prefix would weaken them.
  • NPTv6 maps a /64 to another /64, and ILNP is designed around the /64 boundary.
  • Subnet anycast IIDs reserve at least 7 bits, so a prefix longer than /121 is not possible.
  • An 8-bit IID in a /120 would make SLAAC address collisions highly probable.

The main practical consequence is that deployments with longer prefixes cannot use SLAAC and need manual addresses or DHCPv6.
sections.eli5: Lots of other rules quietly assume the street/house split is in the middle, so moving it would mean fixing all of them.

sections.title: Observed Behaviour and Deployment Issues
sections.content:
A survey of operating systems found that the A bit in the Prefix Information Option is honoured only for a /64 prefix, while the L bit and the Route Information Option work for arbitrary prefix lengths where supported. Forwarding by longest prefix match is expected to work for any length, and some deployments reportedly run /120 subnets using DHCPv6.

Some routers reportedly suffer a performance drop-off or resource exhaustion for prefixes longer than /64, because some chip designs allocate much less space for them. One switch type had a content-addressable memory limited to 144 bits, so the longest prefix in such a filter would be a /112. IPAM tools and management systems would need checking, and a large investment in staff, documents and tools rests on the existing standards.
sections.eli5: Some machines handle long addresses fine, while others slow down or run out of room for them. The existing tools and training also all assume the middle split.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Effects
sections.content:
For privacy, more identifier bits are better. With only 20 bits, just over a million guesses are needed. The RFC argues that at least 40 bits should be available and that prefixes longer than say /80 might raise privacy concerns. A /120 gives the same situation as IPv4 except for the absence of NAT.

For scanning attacks, a longer prefix shrinks the search space, to only 256 addresses for a /120. Any prefix with densely packed addresses is vulnerable, so subnets should be short enough to allow sparse allocation. The RFC calls this ironically the converse of the argument for longer prefixes to resist ND cache attacks.
sections.eli5: If there are only a few possible house numbers, a snoop can try them all. Keeping many possible numbers makes guessing hard.
